screens.title: Advanced Physics Interactions & Optimization
screens.subtitle: Connecting bodies, building ragdolls, and tuning physics for performance

narration.text: In this chapter we'll explore practical techniques that make complex physics feel real while keeping your game fast. You'll learn how Unity's Joints let rigidbodies move together in controlled ways, why the ConfigurableJoint is the go-to tool for lifelike limbs and ragdolls, and how to use the Physics Layer Collision Matrix to limit unnecessary collision checks. We'll also cover optimization tactics: letting rigidbodies sleep, preferring primitive colliders, and when to manually step the physics simulation. A concrete example we'll return to is creating a simple cube-based ragdoll, wiring ConfigurableJoints between bones, and toggling the ragdoll state with a script. That example shows both how joints produce realistic motion and how collider choices and layer filters reduce C P U cost in a busy scene. By the end you'll be able to build physically connected objects, switch an animated character into a ragdoll, and apply a set of clear rules to avoid common performance traps. Ready to see joints and optimizations in action and understand the trade-offs they introduce?

keyIdea.text: Use joints to connect rigidbodies, create ragdolls with ConfigurableJoint, configure collision layers to reduce checks, and apply targeted physics optimizations.

screens.subtitle: Skills you will develop and verify

narration.text: These objectives describe practical skills you'll practice during the lab. First, you'll implement several joint components — hinge, fixed, spring, and configurable — to control how rigidbodies move relative to one another. This matters because choosing the right joint gives predictable behavior for doors, wheels, suspension, or limbs. Second, you'll construct a basic ragdoll using Rigidbody and ConfigurableJoint components. You will rig bones with colliders and enable physics to replace animations on death, which teaches how joints and motion limits produce believable collapse. Third, you'll learn to configure the Physics Layer Collision Matrix so only desired layers perform collision checks; this reduces C P U usage and prevents unwanted interactions like projectiles hitting the player. Fourth, you'll apply optimization techniques such as letting rigidbodies sleep, reducing collider complexity, and selectively adding rigidbodies only where necessary. Each objective includes a short competency milestone so you can verify your work in the Inspector and scene profile. These are practical abilities you will use immediately in gameplay systems and performance tuning.

screens.title: Joints Overview — Hinge, Fixed, Spring, Configurable
screens.subtitle: What each joint does and when to choose it

narration.text: Joints define constraints between two rigidbodies so they move together in controlled ways. A HingeJoint permits rotation around a single axis; use it for doors, wheels, or any part that swings. FixedJoint locks both position and rotation so two objects behave as one, effectively welding them together; it is useful for pieces that should never separate but must stay in one compound body. SpringJoint connects objects with a spring force toward a rest distance, good for elastic connections like simple ropes or suspension. ConfigurableJoint is the flexible powerhouse: it exposes motion and angular axes parameters, limit springs, and motors for each axis. That makes ConfigurableJoint ideal when you need custom limits or want to simulate complex limbs and ragdoll connections. A common misconception is thinking a joint alone produces authentic motion; realistic behavior often requires correct Rigidbody mass, collider placement, and appropriate limit settings. For example, a hinge door needs a Rigidbody on the moving piece and properly tuned mass so the motor or gravity interacts as expected. Key takeaway: match joint capability to the mechanical behavior you need, and test mass, colliders, and limits together to avoid surprising motion.

keyIdea.title: Choose the right joint
keyIdea.text: Select the joint type that matches the desired constraint and tune mass and limits for predictable motion.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Joints Overview
Definition

Joints control relative motion

Joints connect two rigidbodies and constrain linear or angular movement to simulate mechanical links or anatomy.

HingeJoint
Single-axis rotation, supports limits and motors for doors and wheels.
FixedJoint
Locks position and rotation so two bodies move as one.
SpringJoint
Spring-like force between objects, useful for elastic links and suspension.
Key Takeaway

Use simple joints for predictable mechanics and ConfigurableJoint when you need per-axis control.

ConfigurableJoint demo card
Capabilities
  • Lock or free linear X/Y/Z motion
  • Limit angular X/Y/Z motion and set springs
  • Attach motors on axes for active movement
Concrete example
Torso mass = 10, Limb mass = 1. Use ConfigurableJoint angular limits to allow elbow bend while locking twist.
Common mistake
Adding a joint without Rigidbody on both objects or misplacing colliders leads to jitter and unexpected constraints.
Pro tip
Tune mass and limit springs together. A light limb with strong springs will snap back unnaturally.

screens.title: Building a Cube-Based Ragdoll
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step: rig bones, add Rigidbody and colliders, connect with ConfigurableJoint

narration.text: Creating a ragdoll starts with a clear hierarchy and consistent components. First, establish a bone hierarchy: torso as parent, then upper arm, forearm, thigh, and calf as children. Each bone receives a Rigidbody and a simple primitive collider, often a capsule or box; primitive colliders are faster and easier to tune. Second, add a ConfigurableJoint on parent bones and set ConnectedBody to the child's Rigidbody. Configure motion settings: lock linear motions if limbs should keep fixed length, and set angular X, Y, Z limits to mimic real joint ranges. For an elbow, lock Y and Z motion and set X angular limits to permit a natural 0 to -90 degree bend. Third, assign masses thoughtfully—torso heavier than limbs—so gravity and collisions produce realistic collapse. Fourth, keep the ragdoll disabled during normal animation: set rigidbodies to kinematic or disable colliders, then on death disable the animator and enable physics for all parts. A common trap is forgetting to include Rigidbody on both connected objects or using non-convex mesh colliders on moving parts. Follow these steps and iterate on limits and masses until the collapse looks natural.

keyIdea.title: Ragdoll recipe
keyIdea.text: Rig hierarchy → add Rigidbody + primitive colliders → connect with ConfigurableJoint → tune limits and masses → toggle physics at runtime.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Build Ragdoll
Process

Step-by-step ragdoll construction

1. Build bone hierarchy
Create Torso, UpperArm, Forearm, Thigh, Calf as nested transforms.
2. Add Rigidbody and collider
Use Box or Capsule colliders for limbs; prefer primitives for speed.
3. Attach ConfigurableJoint
On the parent, set ConnectedBody to the child and tune linear and angular motions.
4. Tune mass and limits
Give torso higher mass and set angular limits to match limb range.
Key Takeaway

A working ragdoll is the combination of hierarchy, colliders, joints, and tuned masses. Iterate on limits for realism.

Concrete Example
Elbow setup
Attach ConfigurableJoint on UpperArm, ConnectedBody = Forearm Rigidbody. Lock Y/Z motion, set Angular X limit to allow -90 to 0 degrees.
Mass example
Torso mass 10, Limb mass 1–2. Heavier torso prevents limp pieces from flying unrealistically.
Misconception
Using mesh colliders on moving bones looks precise but costs performance and can cause instability; prefer primitives.

screens.title: RagdollActivator Script
screens.subtitle: How the script toggles animation and physics on death

narration.text: The RagdollActivator script provides a simple, reliable way to switch a character from animated control to physics-driven ragdoll. Its essential responsibilities are: keep arrays of the ragdoll's rigidbodies and colliders, initialize the ragdoll in a disabled state, and when Die is called, disable the animator and enable physics on all parts. The script toggles isKinematic and detectCollisions on rigidbodies and enables colliders so the physics engine simulates the pieces. A concrete example: set ragdollRigidbodies to the child rigidbodies in Start by using GetComponentsInChildren, then call SetRagdollState(true) when the character dies. A common error is leaving some rigidbodies kinematic or colliders disabled, which prevents parts from interacting or falling correctly. Another trap is applying large per-frame forces while pieces should be asleep. When you call Die, consider adding a single initial impulse to simulate impact, but avoid repeatedly changing velocities. The core insight is that the animator and kinematic rigidbodies are exclusive control modes; switch cleanly and only once, then let physics run. RagdollActivator Script means disable the animator, make rigidbodies non-kinematic, enable colliders, and optionally apply an initial impulse to simulate impact.. In practical terms, how the script toggles animation and physics on death. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Toggle control cleanly
keyIdea.text: Disable the animator, make rigidbodies non-kinematic, enable colliders, and optionally apply an initial impulse to simulate impact.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › RagdollActivator
Core pattern
Keep arrays of rigidbodies and colliders, initialize ragdoll disabled, and toggle state on Die().
Sample outline
Start: populate ragdollRigidbodies with GetComponentsInChildren.\nSetRagdollState(false).\nOn Die: animator.enabled = false; SetRagdollState(true); optional AddForce impulse.
Common mistake
Forgetting to enable detectCollisions or leaving one Rigidbody as kinematic will cause visual gaps or stuck limbs.
Concrete scenario
Initialization
If arrays are empty, populate them with GetComponentsInChildren in Start to avoid null references.
Die action
Disable Animator, set all rigidbodies isKinematic=false and colliders enabled, then optionally apply a one-time impulse.
Misconception
Calling AddForce repeatedly to simulate collapse creates instability; prefer a single impulse and let physics resolve motion.
Key Takeaway

Switch control cleanly from animator to physics once, ensure all parts are enabled, and avoid per-frame manual velocity writes.

screens.title: Physics Layer Collision Matrix
screens.subtitle: Designing collision rules to reduce checks and unwanted interactions

narration.text: The Physics Layer Collision Matrix is a project-level grid where you declare which physics layers can collide. By default all layers collide, which wastes C P U when many objects share the world but never interact. To use it, create descriptive layers such as Player, Enemy, Projectile, Ragdoll, and StaticEnvironment. Then open Project Settings > Physics and uncheck intersections you do not need. For example, disallow Projectile vs Projectile and Projectile vs Player if projectiles should only hit enemies and environment. This both prevents unwanted gameplay interactions and reduces the number of collision pairs the engine evaluates each physics step. A subtle point: disabling collisions between parts of the same ragdoll can produce smoother motion because limbs won't self-collide, but you must keep Ragoll vs Default enabled for ground interaction. A common misconception is that the Layer Collision Matrix replaces per-object collision rules; it is a coarse, efficient filter—use it in combination with layer masks on raycasts or selective collision toggling for fine control. Physics Layer Collision Matrix means use the layer collision matrix to eliminate whole classes of collision tests and keep only the interactions you need.. In practical terms, designing collision rules to reduce checks and unwanted interactions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Filter collisions early
keyIdea.text: Use the Layer Collision Matrix to eliminate whole classes of collision tests and keep only the interactions you need.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Layer Collision Matrix
Definition
A matrix in Project Settings that defines which layers perform collision checks. Unchecking boxes prevents those layer pairs from colliding at all.
Example configuration
  • Projectile vs Projectile = disabled
  • Projectile vs Player = disabled (if friendly fire off)
  • Ragdoll vs Ragdoll = disabled (optional for smoother limbs)
Concrete scenario
Reducing checks
If 1,000 projectiles are spawned, disabling Projectile vs Projectile stops O(n^2) checks between them and lowers CPU load.
Gameplay control
Preventing projectiles from hitting the player or friendly projectiles creates predictable interactions without per-object checks.
Misconception
Do not rely solely on the matrix for fine-grained per-object filtering; it is a coarse and efficient filter best combined with masks and checks.
Key Takeaway

Plan layers to express interaction categories, then disable unnecessary pairs to save CPU and avoid unintended collisions.

screens.title: Collider Complexity & Rigidbody Count
screens.subtitle: When to use primitive colliders and how many rigidbodies is too many

narration.text: Collider choices and the number of active rigidbodies are two of the most direct levers on physics performance. Primitive colliders—box, sphere, capsule—are fast because they have simple math for collision tests. MeshColliders can be expensive, especially non-convex ones on dynamic objects; they are best reserved for static level geometry. If a moving object needs precision, combine a few primitives to approximate the shape instead of using a mesh collider. Regarding rigidbody count: only give a Rigidbody to objects that must participate in dynamic simulation. Static furniture should be static colliders without Rigidbodies. A common performance bottleneck is hundreds of small rigidbodies that never move but still require per-step checks because they are active. Unity's sleeping mechanic helps, but the best approach is to make truly static objects static or merge them when possible. Concrete example: replace a detailed crate with multiple small mesh colliders by a single box collider and a single Rigidbody when the crate needs to move. Misconception: more rigidbodies equals better collision fidelity—it's a trade-off between accuracy and C P U cost. Collider Complexity & Rigidbody Count means use primitive colliders for dynamic objects, reserve mesh colliders for static geometry, and only add rigidbodies where motion is required.. In practical terms, when to use primitive colliders and how many rigidbodies is too many. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Prefer primitives, minimize Rigidbodies
keyIdea.text: Use primitive colliders for dynamic objects, reserve mesh colliders for static geometry, and only add rigidbodies where motion is required.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Colliders & Rigidbodies
Comparison

Primitive vs MeshCollider

Primitive colliders
Fast and predictable. Combine boxes/capsules for complex shapes.
MeshColliders
Use for static, complex geometry. Avoid non-convex mesh colliders on moving rigidbodies.
Concrete example
Replace many meshes
Swap multiple small mesh colliders on a moving crate for one box collider and a single Rigidbody to lower cost.
Rigidbody count
Only add rigidbodies to objects that need to move or respond to forces. Mark static objects as Static.
Misconception
Turning many parts into rigidbodies for realism can easily overwhelm the physics system; prioritize key interactive items.
Key Takeaway

Accuracy is valuable, but performance matters. Prefer primitives and keep the number of active rigidbodies under control.

screens.title: Sleeping Rigidbodies & When to Wake Them
screens.subtitle: Let physics pause work for rested objects to save CPU

narration.text: Sleeping rigidbodies is Unity's automatic optimization that excludes static or resting rigidbodies from active simulation. When a Rigidbody's velocity and angular velocity fall below thresholds, the engine marks it as sleeping and skips per-step collision resolution until something wakes it. This reduces C P U because sleeping objects do not require continuous constraint solving. Avoid design patterns that constantly wake objects, such as manually zeroing velocities every frame or applying tiny forces each update. If you must wake an object, do it deliberately—apply a single impulse, set velocity, or call WakeUp in response to a clear event. A practical example: in a pile of boxes, only those impacted by the player should wake; avoid sending broadcast forces to the whole pile. A common misconception is treating sleeping as permanent; sleeping objects will awaken when another object collides with them or when you explicitly wake them. Key takeaway: design interactions so objects naturally go to sleep and only wake when needed, which keeps the physics budget low in large scenes. Sleeping Rigidbodies & When to Wake Them means sleeping reduces physics cost. wake objects only in response to meaningful events, not every frame.. In practical terms, let physics pause work for rested objects to save cpu. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Let idle objects sleep
keyIdea.text: Sleeping reduces physics cost. Wake objects only in response to meaningful events, not every frame.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Sleeping Rigidbodies
Definition

What sleeping means

Sleeping excludes resting rigidbodies from per-step simulation until a wake event occurs, saving CPU cycles in complex scenes.
Example
A crate comes to rest and sleeps. When the player pushes it, it wakes and resumes simulation, then may sleep again when settled.
Best practices
Avoid forced wakes
Do not write velocity = zero every frame to prevent sleeping; let physics manage rest.
Wake intentionally
Use WakeUp or apply a single impulse when a real event should reactivate the object.
Misconception
Sleeping objects are not broken; they simply pause until a meaningful interaction occurs.
Key Takeaway

Design interactions so objects can sleep and only wake for genuine events. That keeps physics affordable at scale.

screens.title: Physics.autoSimulation & Manual Simulation
screens.subtitle: Control when physics steps happen for deterministic or timed updates

narration.text: Physics. autoSimulation controls whether Unity automatically runs the physics simulation every FixedUpdate. For most games, leaving auto-simulation on is simpler and correct. However, advanced scenarios such as deterministic simulation, networked physics, or batched physics updates benefit from manual simulation. When you disable auto-simulation, you must call Physics. Simulate with the fixed delta time at the right point in your update loop. This gives you precise control over when collisions and rigidbody updates happen, which can reduce physics cost by running simulation less frequently or only during visible frames. A concrete example is a networked server that runs physics at a controlled tick rate independent of rendering. A common trap is forgetting to call Physics. Simulate each frame after disabling auto-simulation; without calls, nothing moves. Another issue is running Simulate twice per frame or at inconsistent intervals. The key lesson: only disable auto-simulation when you have a clear need for manual timing and you are prepared to manage simulation calls deterministically. Physics.autoSimulation & Manual Simulation means disable auto-simulation only for deterministic or specialized timing; then call physics.simulate reliably each tick.. In practical terms, control when physics steps happen for deterministic or timed updates. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Manual simulation when needed
keyIdea.text: Disable auto-simulation only for deterministic or specialized timing; then call Physics.Simulate reliably each tick.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Manual Simulation
Definition

Physics.autoSimulation

Toggle auto-simulation in Project Settings and manually call Physics.Simulate(Time.fixedDeltaTime) when you need explicit control.
Example call
In your game loop: Physics.Simulate(Time.fixedDeltaTime); // once per physics tick
When to use it
Network servers
Run physics at a fixed tick independent of frame-rate for deterministic behavior.
Batched updates
Control when heavy physics updates occur to avoid spikes during gameplay peaks.
Misconception
Manual simulation is not a cure-all; incorrect timing or missed calls breaks physics entirely.
Key Takeaway

Only disable auto-simulation if you will reliably manage physics ticks; otherwise prefer built-in timing for correctness.

screens.title: Tuning ConfigurableJoint for Ragdoll Limbs
screens.subtitle: Set motions, angular limits, and limit springs to shape limb behavior

narration.text: ConfigurableJoint exposes many properties; tuning them in combination produces believable limb motion. Begin by setting linear motions—XMotion, YMotion, ZMotion—to Locked if you want limbs to keep a fixed length. For angular control, choose the right angular mode: use Angular X/Y/Z Limit to clamp rotations. For an elbow, lock unnecessary axes and set X limits to a range like -90 to 0 degrees. Use Limit Spring values to give joints a gentle return force; higher spring makes the joint stiffer, while damper controls oscillation. Motors can apply active torque if you need controlled movement, but for passive ragdolls focus on limits and springs. Always test with realistic masses and colliders in place; a poorly tuned spring on a very light limb will snap it unnaturally. A common misconception is thinking limits alone create smooth motion. Limits stop extremes but springs and dampers control how the joint moves between limits. Iterate: apply a limit, run the scene, observe the motion, then tweak spring and damper until the limb behaves naturally. Tuning ConfigurableJoint for Ragdoll Limbs means use angular limits to constrain motion and limit springs/damper to control joint stiffness and return behavior.. In practical terms, set motions, angular limits, and limit springs to shape limb behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Tune limits, springs, damper
keyIdea.text: Use angular limits to constrain motion and limit springs/damper to control joint stiffness and return behavior.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Tuning Joints
Tuning steps
  1. Lock linear motion if limb length should remain constant.
  2. Set angular limits to match biological ranges for elbows and knees.
  3. Add limit springs and damper to control stiffness and oscillation.
  4. Test with final masses and colliders, then iterate.
Example
Elbow values
Lock Y/Z rotation, Angular X limit = -90 to 0. Limit Spring: Spring = 50, Damper = 7 for gentle return.
Avoid
Huge springs on very light limbs; this creates snapping and instability.
Misconception
Expecting limits alone to look natural; springs shape movement between limits and control energy dissipation.
Key Takeaway

Tune limits first, then add springs and damper to sculpt natural joint motion; always test with final masses and colliders.

screens.title: Common Performance Bottlenecks & Mitigations
screens.subtitle: Identify typical physics costs and how to reduce them

narration.text: As scenes get complex, a handful of patterns commonly drive physics cost. Too many active rigidbodies leads to heavy per-step processing—mitigate by marking static objects as Static or merging them. Complex mesh colliders, especially non-convex meshes on dynamic objects, are expensive; replace them with primitive colliders or convex mesh colliders when needed. Frequent raycasts and overlap checks can also consume C P U; use LayerMasks and distance limits to restrict queries to relevant targets. Another frequent issue is leaving collision checks enabled between layers that never interact. Use the Layer Collision Matrix to remove those pairs entirely. When diagnosing, use the profiler to spot physics time and test changes iteratively, not all at once. A practical approach: identify the heaviest cost in the profiler, change one element—like switching a mesh collider for a capsule—then re-profile. Misconception: micro-optimizing multiple small items without first profiling often wastes time. Key insight: target the largest cost first, use primitives, reduce active rigidbodies, and apply layer filters to scale physics performance. Common Performance Bottlenecks & Mitigations means use the profiler to find the biggest physics cost, then apply targeted fixes: primitives, fewer rigidbodies, and layer filtering.. In practical terms, identify typical physics costs and how to reduce them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Profile, then fix
keyIdea.text: Use the profiler to find the biggest physics cost, then apply targeted fixes: primitives, fewer rigidbodies, and layer filtering.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Bottlenecks & Fixes
Common bottlenecks
  • Large numbers of active Rigidbody objects
  • Non-convex MeshColliders on dynamic objects
  • Excessive raycasts or overlap checks without masks
  • Unfiltered collision checks between layers
Mitigations
Profile first
Use the Unity profiler to find the heaviest physics cost before changing systems.
Use primitives
Replace mesh colliders on moving parts with boxes, spheres, or capsules.
Layer filtering
Disable unnecessary layer pairs in the Collision Matrix to cut costly checks.
Misconception
Avoid changing many variables at once; iterate and re-profile to confirm improvements.
Key Takeaway

Target the biggest physics costs first: primitives, fewer dynamic bodies, and layer filtering give the largest wins.

screens.title: Hands-on Activity: Create a Simple Ragdoll and Configure Layers
screens.subtitle: A guided checklist to build, test, and optimize a cube-based ragdoll

narration.text: This activity walks you through building a basic ragdoll from cubes and configuring collision layers to prevent unwanted interactions. Start a fresh scene and make a Torso cube with a Rigidbody and BoxCollider. Add child cubes for limbs and give each a Rigidbody and BoxCollider. Set masses: torso heavier, limbs lighter. Add ConfigurableJoint components on parent bones and set ConnectedBody to the child Rigidbody. Lock linear motions and configure angular limits to approximate elbows and knees. In Play mode, disable the ragdoll by making rigidbodies kinematic or disabling colliders. Create a RagdollActivator script on the torso, populate ragdoll arrays in Start, and implement Die to disable animator and call SetRagdollState(true). For layers, create a new layer named Ragdoll and assign the parts. In Project Settings > Physics, uncheck Ragdoll vs Ragdoll to prevent self-collisions, but keep Ragdoll vs Default enabled for ground. Run, trigger Die, and observe. If limbs jitter, verify colliders are not overlapping, masses are reasonable, and limits aren't too tight. This checklist focuses practice on realistic setup and measured optimization. Hands-on Activity: Create a Simple Ragdoll and Configure Layers means follow the build, connect, script, and layer steps to create a working ragdoll and validate layer configuration for performance and behavior.. content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Lab Walkthrough
Checklist
  1. Create Torso cube, add Rigidbody and BoxCollider.
  2. Add limb cubes as children; give each Rigidbody and BoxCollider.
  3. Set torso mass higher, limbs lower.
  4. Add ConfigurableJoint on parent, ConnectedBody = child Rigidbody.
  5. Lock linear motions, set angular limits for joints.
  6. Create RagdollActivator, populate arrays, toggle ragdoll on input.
  7. Create Ragdoll layer and edit Layer Collision Matrix as needed.
Troubleshooting
Jitter fix
Ensure colliders don't start overlapping, check for missing rigidbodies, and reduce spring strength if oscillation occurs.
No collapse
Confirm animator is disabled when ragdoll is active and rigidbodies are non-kinematic with colliders enabled.
Layer issues
If parts pass through each other or ground, check Layer Collision Matrix entries and collider enable states.
Key Takeaway

Follow the steps, then iterate on limits, masses, and colliders until the ragdoll behaves naturally and performs well.

Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Key Concepts
Joints

Components that define relative motion between rigidbodies such as Hinge, Fixed, Spring, and Configurable.

ConfigurableJoint

Most versatile joint, allowing fine control over linear and angular motion, limits, and springs along each axis.

Ragdoll Physics

Use Rigidbody and ConfigurableJoint on bones to simulate realistic collapse; toggle physics by disabling Animator and enabling rigidbodies.

Summary: Use joints intentionally, tune masses and limits, and switch control cleanly between animator and physics.

narration.text: These final concept cards focus on performance and common optimizations. The Physics Layer Collision Matrix is a coarse but powerful filter: disable layer pairs to avoid unnecessary collision checks. Sleeping Rigidbodies saves C P U by excluding settled objects from active simulation; design interactions so objects sleep when appropriate and wake only for real events. Collider complexity matters: primitive colliders are cheap; non-convex MeshColliders on dynamic objects are expensive and unstable. Finally, Physics. autoSimulation can be disabled for deterministic or networked scenarios, but manual simulation requires careful, consistent calls to Physics. Simulate. Keep these practices in mind: profile before optimizing, prefer primitives and layer filtering, and manage rigidbody counts to scale physics performance. keyIdea.title: Optimize smartly
keyIdea.text: Use layer filters, sleeping, primitive colliders, and careful simulation control to reduce physics cost and maintain realism.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Optimization
Layer Matrix

Disable unnecessary layer collisions to cut down the number of pair checks the physics engine performs.

Sleeping

Allow objects to sleep naturally and wake them only for meaningful events to reduce per-step cost.

Collider Complexity

Prefer primitive colliders for dynamic objects; reserve complex meshes for static geometry only.

Final summary: profile first, then apply primitives, layer filters, sleeping, and managed simulation to keep physics performant and predictable.
